title: Tables, rows and keys
summary: What a relational database really is: tables of typed facts, a key that names every row, and keys that link rows together.
youWillLearn: Why apps outgrow "one big file" and what a database does instead
How tables, rows and columns map to the things in your app
What a primary key is, and why it should never mean anything
How a foreign key links a note to its owner, and guards that link

glossary.relational database: A database that stores data in tables and links rows across tables by their keys. Postgres is one.
glossary.Postgres: PostgreSQL, a free and very widely used relational database. Every Supabase project is a Postgres database.
glossary.table: A named collection of rows that all describe the same kind of thing, like users or notes.
glossary.row: One entry in a table: one user, one note. Also called a record.
glossary.column: One named, typed fact that every row in a table has, like title or created_at.
glossary.primary key: The column whose value is unique for every row and never changes, so the row can always be found again.
glossary.uuid: A long random id like 3f9c2a1e-…, practically impossible to guess or to repeat by accident.
glossary.foreign key: A column that stores the primary key of a row in another table, and that the database checks really exists.
glossary.constraint: A rule declared on a column or table, like not null or unique, that the database enforces on every write.

steps.title: One big file stops working fast
body: Say Notely's first version saves every note into one big notes.json file. For Maya alone, it works.

Then real users arrive. To show Maya her notes, the server reads every note anyone ever wrote. Two saves land at the same moment and one is lost. Two notes are both called "Groceries", and nothing says whose is whose.

callout.text: A shoebox of receipts. Fine for ten. With ten thousand, finding "March, Maya, groceries" means tipping the whole box on the floor.

scene.caption: Every request reads and rewrites the whole file. It gets slow, and saves collide.

notes.text: To find one note, read them all
Two saves at once: one is lost

steps.title: A database is a set of tidy tables
body: A relational database stores data in tables, one table per kind of thing: users, notes, later tags.

It also does the hard parts for you: finding things fast, letting many people write at once without losing anything, and refusing data that breaks your rules. Every Supabase project is one of these: Postgres.

callout.text: You met replication and sharding in system design. Those are ways to run many copies or pieces of this same database. This module is about what goes inside one.

scene.caption: The file is gone. Postgres keeps one table per kind of thing.

steps.title: Rows are things, columns are facts
body: Picture a spreadsheet with stricter rules. Each row is one thing: one note. Each column is one fact about it: its title, its owner, when it was made.
Unlike a spreadsheet, every column has a fixed type. A created_at column only takes dates, so a stray "next week-ish" cannot sneak in.

scene.caption: The notes table: three columns, one row per note.

steps.title: Every row needs a name tag
body: Two notes can share a title, so the title cannot tell them apart. Each table gets a primary key: one column, usually id, whose value is unique and never changes.
The database guarantees it. Try to insert a second row with id 101 and it refuses. Ids are usually numbers the database counts up, or a random uuid.

scene.caption: Id 101 is taken, so the database refuses the duplicate row.

steps.title: Keys that point at other tables
body: How does a note know it belongs to Maya? It stores her id in a column called user_id. A column that holds another table's primary key is a foreign key.
Declare it, and Postgres guards the link: it will not save a note for user 99 if user 99 does not exist. These links are the "relational" in relational database.

scene.caption: Each note row points at exactly one user row through user_id.

steps.title: Notely's first two tables in SQL
body: Here is the whole idea as real code. Paste it into the Supabase SQL editor and you get both tables, both primary keys and the link between them.
Read each line like a form field: name, type, then rules such as not null (must be filled) and unique (no repeats). Rules like these are called constraints.

code.caption: References users (id) is the foreign key. Real Supabase apps get users from Supabase Auth, with uuid ids; lesson 6 shows how.

scene.caption: Two create table statements: two tables, two primary keys, one foreign key.

steps.title: Do not use a fact as the key
body: Tempting: make Maya's email the primary key of users. It is unique, after all.

Then Maya changes her email. Every note that stored the old address must change too, or the database refuses the update. Keys should be boring values with no meaning, so they never need to change. Keep the email as a normal column with a unique rule.

callout.text: When Claude Code creates tables, check: does every table have a primary key? Is each link a real references foreign key, not a plain column that happens to hold an id? Are required columns not null? Ask it to show the final create table SQL, even if it used a dashboard or an ORM.

scene.caption: If the email were the key, changing it would break every note that points at it.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A relational database is a set of tables. Rows are things, columns are typed facts. A primary key names each row for good. A foreign key stores another row's key, and the database keeps those links honest.
The rest of this module, from joins to migrations, builds on these four ideas.

scene.caption: Tables, rows, a key on every row, and checked links between them.

quiz.question: Notely's notes table has the columns id, user_id and title. Which one is the foreign key?

options.why: That is the primary key: it names this note. It does not point anywhere else.
It stores the primary key of a row in another table, users. That is exactly what a foreign key is.
The title is an ordinary fact about the note. Two notes can even share one.

quiz.question: Claude Code proposes a users table whose primary key is the email column. What do you ask for?

options.text: Keep it. Emails are unique, so they make a fine key.
options.why: Unique is not enough. A key must also never change, and people change their email.

options.text: Drop the unique rule on email, so changing it is easier.
options.why: That would allow two accounts with the same email. The fix is a different key, not a weaker rule.

options.text: A generated id as the primary key, and email as a unique column.
options.why: The id has no meaning, so it never needs to change. Email stays unique, and can change without breaking any links.

quiz.question: A bug in Notely tries to save a note with user_id = 99, but there is no user 99. The foreign key is declared. What happens?

options.text: Postgres rejects the insert with an error.
options.why: A foreign key means the referenced row must exist. The bad write never lands, so the bug shows up instead of hiding.

options.text: The note is saved and simply never shows up for anyone.
options.why: That is what happens without a foreign key: orphan rows that quietly pile up.

options.text: Postgres creates an empty user 99 to keep things consistent.
options.why: Databases never invent rows for you. A constraint can only accept or refuse a write.

takeaways: A relational database is a set of tables: one per kind of thing, one row per thing, one typed column per fact.
Every table needs a primary key: unique, never changing, with no meaning of its own.
A foreign key (references) links rows across tables, and Postgres refuses links to rows that do not exist.
Put rules like not null and unique in the database, not only in app code.
